readings.title: 出没的大猫
readings.text: Reports of a strange animal began to accumulate in the spring. Farmers claimed that sheep had been killed, and a shopkeeper swore he had spotted a large cat crossing the road at dawn. The newspaper called it 'the beast of Willow Valley', and soon everyone was talking about it. Police at first dismissed the stories, but when grey fur was found on a fence, they agreed to investigate. An animal expert was invited from the city. He examined the prints carefully and measured them twice. 'This is no tiger,' he announced, to the disappointment of the reporters. 'But it is certainly no ordinary house cat either.' Volunteers organized night watches. For three weeks nothing happened. Then, on a rainy Tuesday, the mystery ended quietly: the beast walked into a barn, ate two bowls of milk, and fell asleep beside the farm dog. It was Max, an enormous pet cat who had been missing — and living very well — for two months.

questions.q: What made the police change their minds?
What did the expert conclude?
options: It was neither tiger nor ordinary house cat

questions.q: How did the story end?
options: Max the pet cat was found well-fed
The cat escaped to the hills

readings.title: 敲了十三下的钟
readings.text: The town clock had kept perfect time for eighty years — until one June evening, when it struck thirteen. Tourists arrived the next day with cameras. Journalists rang the mayor's office. The occasion might have delighted the town council, had the mayor not been eager to prove it never happened. An engineer was sent to examine the mechanism, and the poor caretaker, Mr. Bell, was asked the same question forty times: 'Did you wind it twice?' Mr. Bell, a man of sincere honesty, acknowledged nothing and admitted nothing. He simply smiled. The engineer found nothing wrong. The mystery remained until autumn, when a reporter finally checked the old newspapers of exactly one hundred years before. On the same June evening a century earlier, the clock had struck thirteen too — and the town, back then, had sold thousands of postcards celebrating it. Mr. Bell, it turned out, knew the story all along. Some traditions, he said quietly, deserve to repeat themselves once a century.

questions.q: Why was the mayor unhappy?
options: He wanted to prove it never happened

questions.q: How did Mr. Bell answer questions?
What did the old newspapers reveal?
options: The clock struck thirteen a century ago
Mr. Bell's grandfather stole the bell

readings.title: 灯塔守者的风暴
readings.text: For thirty-one years, old Anders had kept the lighthouse burning, and in all that time he had never once failed. So when the radio warned of the worst storm in decades, he simply nodded, checked his lamp, and made tea. The gale arrived at midnight. Waves exploded against the tower; the wind tore at the roof like a living thing. At two o'clock the electric supply failed, and Anders climbed the stairs with a heavy oil can, step by step, gradually fighting both gravity and age. By dawn the lamp still burned. In the harbour below, a fishing boat — guided safely through the black water — reached the pier. Its crew never learned the keeper's name, and he never told them. When reporters asked him later whether he had been afraid, the old man thought for a moment. 'Fear is natural,' he said. 'So is responsibility. You simply decide which of the two will climb the stairs with you.' Then he went back to polishing the lamp.

questions.q: What failed at two o'clock?
How did the fishing boat get home safely?
What does Anders say about fear and duty?
options: You choose which one climbs with you

readings.title: 为河流的一小时
readings.text: Nobody remembered who first suggested it, but on the first Sunday of May, half the town appeared at the riverbank carrying gloves and rubbish bags. The idea was simple: give the river one hour. Students, shopkeepers, and two reluctant teenagers dragged in by their mothers formed teams along the water. At nine o'clock the campaign began, and by ten the banks looked transformed. Tyres, bottles, and a truly astonishing quantity of plastic bags left the reeds where they had rested for years. One volunteer fished out a bicycle; another found a wedding photo, still in its frame, which was returned to a blushing couple married twenty years before. The mayor gave a short speech about protecting the environment; the crowd politely applauded and then returned to picking up litter, which everyone privately agreed was the more useful speech. Since that day, the hour has become a local custom. The river, for its part, has answered in its own way — with kingfishers returning to the reeds each spring.

questions.q: What was the plan?
options: To give the river one hour of cleaning

readings.title: 周二来的信
readings.text: Mei had applied for the scholarship mostly to silence her uncle, who insisted that girls from small towns should not hunt for big dreams. She wrote the essay at the kitchen table between dinner shifts, describing her grandmother, who traded vegetables for piano lessons. When the envelope arrived on a plain Tuesday, she nearly filed it unopened under 'another polite refusal'. Inside, however, was a single page: she had been awarded the full grant. Her mother cried into the soup. Her uncle, to his credit, was the first to congratulate her, though he added that it would probably be very tiring. It was. Three years later, standing on a hospital ward as a newly qualified doctor, Mei still kept the envelope in her desk drawer — not as proof of her achievement, but as a reminder of her grandmother trading tomatoes for scales. Talent, she had learned, rarely announces itself loudly. Sometimes it whispers from a kitchen table, waiting for somebody stubborn enough to listen.

questions.q: Why did Mei first apply?
options: To win a prize for writing

questions.q: Who was first to congratulate her?
Why does she keep the envelope?
options: As a reminder of her grandmother's trade

readings.title: 外婆的笔记本
readings.text: When Grandmother died, we expected lawyers and paperwork. Instead, we found a fat notebook wrapped in cloth, its pages soft with age. Inside were recipes — but written like letters: 'Add salt when the soup stops asking for it.' 'Stir slowly, the way you walk when you are happy.' At first we laughed. Then my sister, who had inherited none of Grandmother's cooking talent, attempted the New Year dumplings strictly following the strange instructions. They tasted exactly right, though nobody could explain why. Word spread among the cousins, and soon the notebook travelled from kitchen to kitchen like a honoured guest. We began adding our own pages — my brother recorded how to fix a bicycle chain, my aunt noted remedies for homesickness. Last winter, a neighbour's daughter asked if she might copy a few pages for her own future family. Of course, we said. A heritage that is hidden away is merely storage; a heritage that is shared becomes a tradition. Grandmother, who shared everything, would have approved of the stains on the newest pages.

questions.q: What was in the notebook?
How did the sister's dumplings turn out?
What is the story's point?
options: Hidden heritage is mere storage; shared, it becomes tradition

readings.title: 12路公交车上的钱包
readings.text: Old Chen drove Bus 12 for twenty-two years and claimed he had seen everything. So when he spotted a leather wallet glowing under a seat after the last run, he was neither excited nor troubled. He logged it, locked it in the depot safe, and went home to his noodles. The wallet belonged to a young nurse named Lin, and it held her first month's salary in cash — savings meant for her mother's medicine. She came to the depot the next morning, pale and prepared for the worst. Instead, a sleepy clerk produced the wallet, counted every bill in front of her, and had her sign a form. Nothing was missing. Lin tried to offer a reward; Old Chen waved it away with genuine offence. 'The seat belongs to the bus,' he said, 'and the bus belongs to the route, and the route belongs to everybody.' Years later, Nurse Lin tells the story to frightened patients before operations. Honesty, she explains, is rarely dramatic. Mostly it is a tired driver, a locked safe, and noodles going cold at home.

questions.q: What did Old Chen do with the wallet?
options: Logged and locked it in the safe

questions.q: Why was the money important to Lin?
What does the story say about honesty?
options: It is often quiet and ordinary

readings.title: 四十二公里
readings.text: At kilometre thirty-five, Daniel's knee announced its formal objection. Every training manual says this is the moment champions are separated from everyone else; what the manuals omit is that most runners simply negotiate. Daniel bargained shamelessly. Run to the next bridge, he promised his leg, and you may stop forever. At the bridge he promised it a hotel breakfast. Somewhere near kilometre forty, promises exhausted, he discovered something quieter than bargaining: the thought of his daughter waiting at the finish with a crayon drawing of 'Daddy flying'. He did not sprint. He did not smile for photographs. He moved forward the way rain falls — steadily, and without drama. The clock read four hours and fifty-one minutes when he crossed the line, far from the leaders. His daughter graded the performance excellent. Only later did he understand what the race had taught him: obstacles are rarely defeated in one heroic blow. They are overcome by agreement — one bridge, one promise, one slow kilometre at a time — by people who persist after the excitement has gone.

questions.q: What happened at kilometre thirty-five?
options: His knee began to hurt badly

questions.q: What finally pushed him forward?
options: His daughter waiting with a drawing

questions.q: What lesson does he draw?
options: Obstacles fall to one heroic blow
Obstacles are overcome bit by bit

readings.title: 读书的村庄
readings.text: The library began as a joke: twelve donated books on a bench outside the post office, protected from rain by an upturned bucket. The postmaster, Mr. Osei, lent them out on trust — no cards, no fines, only the rule that a borrower must tell him one thing they learned. Villagers found the rule irresistible. The farmer reported that Napoleon had been short; his wife disputed this hotly and borrowed a second book to win the argument. Within a year the bench held three hundred volumes, and the bucket had been replaced by a proper wooden case carved by a proud grandfather. Children did homework there after dark because the case sat under the streetlamp. Exam results crept upward; so, more interestingly, did attendance at village meetings, where people had begun, dangerously and delightfully, to ask for evidence. When a journalist came to write about 'rural poverty', Mr. Osei served her tea and handed her a history of the region. 'We are not a poor village,' he corrected mildly. 'We were a quiet one. It has been a decade of noise ever since.'

questions.q: What was the borrowing rule?
options: Tell Mr. Osei one thing learned

questions.q: Why did children sit by the book case at night?
How did Mr. Osei correct the journalist?

readings.title: 平凡英雄
readings.text: Judy never asked to be called brave. For eight years her job was simply to walk ahead of Tom and keep him safe — Tom, who had lost his sight at nineteen, and Judy, a golden retriever with a professional calm and a private weakness for sausage rolls. Their routine was precise: the office by eight, the bakery avoided on Mondays (delivery vans), the canal path avoided always (no railing). One November evening a lorry jumped the curb on Bridge Street, and everything Judy had rehearsed for years happened in four seconds. She pulled Tom back with all her weight, turned him, and pushed him against the wall while the world clattered. Tom broke a wrist; Judy broke nothing but her composure for exactly one minute, trembling against his coat before resuming her dignified post at his knee. Newspapers called her a hero and printed her photograph, which she endured with visible boredom. Tom understood better. Loyalty, he told the reporters, is not one dramatic act. It is the same quiet act repeated eight thousand mornings, until the morning it saves your life.

questions.q: What was Judy's job?
Which route did they always avoid?
What does Tom say loyalty really is?
